text_blocks.snippet: Exercises for labyrinthitis, also known as vestibular rehabilitation exercises, focus on helping the brain adapt to the inner ear's impaired function and improving balance. These exercises, often guided by a physical therapist or audiologist, can include head and eye movement exercises, balance retraining, and canalith repositioning maneuvers for BPPV (Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo).
snippet_highlighted_words: head and eye movement exercises, balance retraining, and canalith repositioning maneuvers for BPPV (Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo)

list.title: Head and Eye Movement Exercises:
list.snippet: These exercises involve specific head movements, like bending, turning, and looking in different directions, while focusing on a fixed point. They help retrain the vestibular system to better coordinate head and eye movements.

list.title: Balance Retraining Exercises:
list.snippet: These exercises, like standing with feet closer together or walking with head turns, challenge and improve balance, helping the body adapt to the impaired inner ear.

list.title: Canalith Repositioning Maneuvers:
list.snippet: If BPPV is a contributing factor, maneuvers like the Epley maneuver or Brandt-Daroff exercises can help reposition displaced crystals in the inner ear.

list.title: Brandt-Daroff Exercises:
list.snippet: Involve moving from a sitting position to lying on one side, then returning to sitting, and repeating on the other side.

list.title: Epley Maneuver:
list.snippet: A series of head and body movements performed while sitting, lying down, and turning the head, designed to reposition canaliths.

list.title: Walking with head turns:
list.snippet: Walking while gently turning the head from side to side, gradually increasing the speed and complexity.

list.title: Standing balance exercises:
list.snippet: Practicing standing with feet closer together, or even attempting tandem stance (heel to toe) to challenge stability.

list.title: Gaze stabilization exercises:
list.snippet: Focusing on a target while moving the head, to improve the ability to maintain focus during head movements.

list.title: Consult a professional:
list.snippet: It's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional (physical therapist, audiologist, or ENT) for proper diagnosis and guidance on appropriate exercises.

list.title: Start slowly:
list.snippet: Begin with exercises that are comfortable and gradually increase the difficulty as symptoms improve.

list.title: Listen to your body:
list.snippet: Stop and rest if symptoms worsen during an exercise and don't push yourself beyond your limits.

list.title: Be patient:
list.snippet: Vestibular rehabilitation can take time, and it's important to be patient and consistent with the exercises.

list.title: Avoid sudden movements:
list.snippet: Minimize sudden head movements and try to keep your head and body movements smooth and controlled.

list.title: Consider using a rating scale:
list.snippet: To track your progress and adjust exercises accordingly, you can use a symptom rating scale to assess the severity of your dizziness or vertigo.
